analysis.one_liner: Expands federal compensation for cancer victims of nuclear testing fallout and uranium mining.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced January 24, 2025 by Sen. Josh Hawley with six original cosponsors from both parties, has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no committee or floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reauthorize and expand a federal program that pays money to people who developed cancer after exposure to radiation from atomic bomb testing, uranium mining, or Manhattan Project radioactive waste. It raises payments to $100,000 for many claimants, adds new affected areas including ZIP codes in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, Kentucky, and Guam, and lets former uranium workers with mixed job histories qualify. It also lengthens the window to file claims from two years to five and allows denied claims to be resubmitted.
analysis.who_benefits: People with specified cancers who lived downwind of atmospheric nuclear tests (including the Trinity test in New Mexico and tests affecting Guam), people who lived in areas contaminated by Manhattan Project waste in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky, and former uranium miners, millers, core drillers, and ore transporters, plus their surviving spouses and children. Survivors of someone who died can claim $25,000; living claimants get the greater of $50,000 or more, plus documented out-of-pocket medical costs in waste-area cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwinders, uranium miners, and waste-area cancer victims

how_it_helps.text: Raises the standard payment for leukemia and other covered cancers linked to atmospheric testing to $100,000, up from $50,000-$75,000 under prior law.

Extends the dates of qualifying exposure for atmospheric testing claims to November 6, 1962, adding downwinders of the Trinity test in New Mexico and exposure periods covering tests in the Pacific, including Guam.

Creates a new compensation category for people who lived at least two years in ZIP codes contaminated by Manhattan Project waste in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky, paying living claimants at least $50,000, surviving spouses or children $25,000, and reimbursing documented out-of-pocket medical expenses.

Expands uranium-worker eligibility to core drillers and mine/mill remediation workers, adds kidney cancer and chronic renal disease as covered conditions, allows combined work histories across mining jobs, and extends the covered employment period from 1971 to 1990.

Extends the filing window for claims from two years to five years after enactment, lets denied claimants resubmit up to three times, and allows people already paid under old, lower amounts to receive the difference.
Expands eligibility under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program for Department of Energy and uranium-workforce employees with cancer.

Funds $3 million per year (2025-2027) in grants for universities to study health effects of uranium mining and milling on people without workplace exposure, including miners' family members, and directs the GAO to study unmet medical coverage needs of test-exposure victims.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Justice Department's Radiation Exposure Compensation trust fund, which the bill extends for six more years. There is no payment from the mining companies or agencies that caused the exposure; the government pays as a matter of recognized liability for its own nuclear weapons program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via the compensation fund

drawbacks.text: Payments are presumptive, not case-by-case proof of causation: claimants qualify by showing residence or work history in an affected area plus a covered disease, not by proving radiation caused their individual cancer. That means some payments will go to people whose illness may have had other causes, the accepted tradeoff for a program victims can navigate without litigation.
The cost is open-ended for taxpayers: the trust fund is extended six years and eligibility, payout amounts, and covered areas all expand, with no funding ceiling stated in the bill.

Proof requirements remain demanding. Manhattan Project waste claimants must document two years of physical presence with contemporaneous records, which can exclude people who moved frequently or lack old paperwork, though the bill allows affidavits and tribal records as alternatives for testing and uranium claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: lump-sum payments that require no lawyer and no lawsuit for people the government itself exposed to radiation, in some cases decades ago and now elderly or deceased. The costs are a presumptive-compensation tradeoff (some overpayment is built in by design) and a taxpayer-funded liability with no stated ceiling. On balance the design favors speed and accessibility for victims over precision, which is a defensible choice for a program compensating past, irreversible harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 24, 2025, and no further action appears in the record.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 24, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
Those are the only two actions listed in the bill's history; no committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote has been recorded.

It was introduced on a bipartisan basis by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) together with Sens. Luján, Heinrich, Kelly (D), Schmitt (R-MO), and Crapo (R-ID), and has 8 total cosponsors (6 Democrats, 2 Republicans).
The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill could still advance if the committee or Senate leadership acts on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has come out ahead: with no vote taken, the expanded compensation has not been enacted and people who qualify under current, narrower rules remain subject to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; claimants still wait

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan original cosponsors from states affected by nuclear testing waste and uranium mining.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor representing New Mexico, home to Trinity test downwinders and uranium mining communities.

for.name: Sens. Martin Heinrich and Mark Kelly
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors from uranium-mining and downwind states.

for.name: Sens. Mike Crapo and Eric Schmitt
for.what_they_did: Joined as original Republican cosponsors, adding bipartisan weight from Idaho and Missouri.

for.name: Additional cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, keeping the bill bipartisan.

against.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and, per the action record, has taken no further action on it; no markup or vote has been scheduled. Because the Congress is still in session, this is a stall rather than a final block.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is split across both parties: a Republican lead sponsor from Missouri with six of eight cosponsors Democratic, drawn from states with downwinder and uranium-mining communities; no opposition has been recorded in the bill's history.

industries.industry: Federal taxpayers (via the DOJ compensation trust fund)
industries.note: The bill extends the trust fund six years, raises payouts to $100,000, and adds new claimant groups, increasing federal outlays. This cost is the funding mechanism for the compensation itself, so the taxpayers' interest here runs alongside the beneficiaries'.

industries.industry: Institutions of higher education and research nonprofits
industries.note: The bill authorizes $3 million per year for fiscal 2025-2027 in grants, administered by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, to study uranium mining and milling health effects among non-occupationally exposed people.

industries.industry: Alaska universities, tribal organizations, and nonprofits near the Amchitka site
industries.note: The bill directs the Energy Department to award a cooperative agreement, by September 30, 2025, to a qualifying Alaska association to support long-term monitoring of the Amchitka nuclear test site, incorporating Indigenous knowledge and local tribal participation.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to committee never get a vote, and months into the session this one has no committee action on the record. Its bipartisan sponsorship from senators of affected states gives it a path if the Judiciary Committee or Senate leadership schedules it, but unless pressure from downwinder, uranium-worker, and waste-area communities forces action, the likely outcome is that it remains pending and may need to be reintroduced in a future Congress.
